why: The base has the answer mode but rarely selects it without the prompt cue.
The cue already flips the switch, so a quarter of the delta, which mostly duplicates the switch, adds little to the cued base's 410.
At a = 0.5 the switch is saturated by the delta alone (about 432 plain), so the cue adds almost nothing on top.
RL already sits in the mode the cue selects, so the cue leaves RL at its plain score of 463.
The Code-RL delta carries part of the same switch, which the cue already flips, so Code-RL with the cue lands near the cued base's 410.
A random direction carries no switch component; with the cue on, it lands at or slightly below the cued base.
Accuracy is sharply concave in delta scale, so a quarter of the delta flips most of the switch and recovers about three quarters of the 224 -> 463 gain.
Half the delta saturates the switch, as each half of the matrices did in n13, recovering about 85 % of the gain.
Code-RL writes part of the same answer-mode direction (cue token in its late readouts), so it lifts the plain base well above 224 on math without math training.
A mode switch along one direction is largely a constant shift in the residual stream, so one vector per layer closes a substantial share of KL even on cued text.
On RL text the mode shift is the main difference, so one constant vector per layer closes more of the KL than on cued-base text.
The switch is spread over MLP and attention redundantly, so the MLP-only constant vector closes most of what the full vector does.
Same redundancy on RL text: the MLP-only constant vector closes most of the full constant vector's share.
